Trace Elements Trace elements are inorganic substances found in small amounts in the tissues and required for various meta- bolic processes; together with the vitamins (see below) they are sometimes referred to as micronutrients. The elements considered essential are chromium, copper, fluorine, iodine, iron, manganese, molybdenum, sele- nium, and zinc. Iron, in the form of haem, plays an es- sential role in oxygen transport while iodine is required by the thyroid for the formation of thyroid hormones; most of the other essential trace elements are cofactors for various enzymes. Boron, nickel, silicon, and vana- dium may also be essential, and it has been suggested on the basis of animal studies that there might be a re- quirement for tin. Well-defined deficiency syndromes exist for copper, iodine, iron, selenium, and zinc; although deficiency of other trace elements is possible, their deficiency syn- dromes are not well defined because of their ubiquity in the diet. Guidance concerning the intake of various trace elements has been published—see also Human Requirements under Vitamins, below. ◊ References. 1. WHO. Trace elements in human nutrition and health.
